analysis.one_liner: Lets tipped workers deduct up to $25,000 of reported tips from federal income tax.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it unanimously on May 20, 2025, but the House has not voted and the bill sits at the House desk.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal income tax deduction of up to $25,000 for cash tips that workers report to their employer for tax withholding [S2][S3]. It covers people in occupations that customarily received tips before 2024, and it phases out for workers who earned more than $160,000 from that employer the prior year [S2][S3]. It also expands an existing business tax credit — which refunds employers the payroll taxes they pay on their employees' tips — to cover barbers, nail salons, estheticians, and spa workers, not just restaurants [S2][S3]. The deduction would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2024 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers — servers, bartenders, hairstylists, nail techs, valets and similar — who pay federal income tax and whose tips are reported to their employer. A server making $30,000 with $10,000 in reported tips would owe income tax on roughly $20,000 instead of $30,000. Employers in the beauty and spa trades gain a new tax credit for the payroll taxes they pay on their workers' tips. Non-itemizers can claim the deduction, so workers who don't itemize still get it [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a deduction of up to $25,000 for cash tips that workers report to their employer, available to all taxpayers including those who do not itemize [S2][S3].
Excludes high earners: workers who made over $160,000 from that employer in the prior year cannot claim the tip deduction [S2][S3].
Requires Treasury to adjust withholding tables so workers see the benefit in their paychecks during the year, not just at filing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which would collect less income tax — about the cost of the lost revenue. Workers would still owe payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare) on their tips. Some low-income workers who owe little or no federal income tax would get little or no benefit, because a deduction lowers taxable income rather than handing back money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury through lost tax revenue

drawbacks.text: Only tips reported to the employer for withholding count, and the deduction is limited to cash tips — so the size of the benefit depends on what is actually reported [S2][S3].
A deduction helps only people who owe income tax. A tipped worker with very low income gets little or nothing, unlike a refundable credit would [S2].
Workers still pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on tips; the bill touches income tax only [S2].
The employer payroll-tax credit for tips is extended to beauty and spa businesses, a tax break for employers layered on top of the worker deduction [S2][S3].
Making tips tax-free increases their after-tax value, which can reinforce tip-based pay structures rather than wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tipped workers, the benefit is real and immediate: a deduction worth several hundred to a few thousand dollars a year for millions of people, with a high-income cap that keeps it targeted. The main costs are the lost federal revenue and the design quirks — cash-only, reported-tips-only, no help for those who owe little tax, and an employer credit on top. It does nothing about the underlying tipped minimum wage. On balance it is a genuine, if imperfect, tax cut for working people.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously in May 2025, but the House has taken no vote; the bill was received and held at the desk.

narrative.text: Introduced January 16, 2025 by Sen. Ted Cruz and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S1][S5].
The Finance Committee discharged the bill and the Senate passed it without amendment by unanimous consent on May 20, 2025 — no roll-call vote, no recorded opposition [S5].
The bill was sent to the House on May 23, received May 26, and held at the desk; the House has taken no further action [S5].
Congress is still in session, so the bill could in principle still receive House action before January 2027 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost much: the Senate passed the bill with no opposition, and the current law taxing tips remains in effect while the House takes no action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; tip tax persists

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to Senate passage by unanimous consent.

for.name: Senate cosponsors (6 of 55 Senate Republicans, 2 of 45 Senate Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing from the start.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Discharged the bill by unanimous consent on May 20, 2025, letting it skip a markup and go straight to the floor.

for.name: The full Senate
for.role: Passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on May 20, 2025
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill with no recorded votes against it.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 26, 2025 and held it at the desk; no vote has been scheduled [S5]. Widely reported that the House instead adopted a tip-deduction provision inside its larger tax bill, leaving this standalone version unaddressed.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition, and its 8 cosponsors split 6 Republicans and 2 Democrats; the only delay has been House inaction, not a party fight.

industries.industry: Beauty, barbering, nail and spa businesses
industries.note: The bill extends the existing employer tip payroll-tax credit to these establishments, so salon and spa owners get a new tax break alongside their workers' deduction [S2][S3].

Restaurant employers keep their existing tip payroll-tax credit, and tax-free tips make tip-based pay more attractive, reinforcing a wage system built on customer tips rather than employer wages [S2].

Workers in occupations that customarily receive tips get up to $25,000 of income excluded from federal income tax, as long as the tips are reported and they earn under $160,000 from that employer [S2][S3].

analysis.trajectory: The House has held the bill at its desk since May 26, 2025 with no scheduled vote. A nearly identical tip deduction was included in the large tax law signed in July 2025 (applying through 2028), which is widely reported; that makes House action on this standalone Senate bill unlikely, and it may simply sit until the Congress ends. If the enacted version's provision were ever allowed to lapse, this bill could be revived.
